panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 9 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I). A: Real patient colonoscopic image from the CURE hematochezia cohort showing erythema and edematous mucosa, a mild mucosal ischemic injury pattern explicitly listed in the caption and in-text as a transient/reversible ischemic colitis finding. B: Real patient colonoscopic image showing patchy erythema, petechial hemorrhage, and pale areas; petechial hemorrhage is a named vocabulary finding and matches the in-text description of mucosal ischemic injury. C: Real patient colonoscopic image of a superficial longitudinal ulcer, the characteristic single-stripe longitudinal ulceration pattern of ischemic colitis described in the caption and in-text. D: Real patient colonoscopic image showing an irregularly shaped ulcer, consistent with a deeper non-necrotic ischemic ulceration pattern in the caption's severity spectrum. E: Real patient colonoscopic image showing scattered deep ulcerations, matching the deeper submucosal ischemic...

panels.figure_caption: Recommended classification of ischemic colitis for risk stratification during colonoscopy. (A) Erythema and edematous mucosa; (B) Patchy erythema, petechial hemorrhage, and pale area; (C) Superficial longitudinal ulcer; (D) Irregularly shaped ulcer; (E) Scattered deep ulcerations; (F) Scattered ulcerations and mucosal edema along the longitudinal axis of the colon; (G) Near semi-circumferential ulcer; (H) Diffuse mucosal congestion and hemorrhage; and (I) Cyanotic mucosa and pseudopolyps [18,23]. [Colonoscopic images were from patients who previously enrolled in the CURE severe hematochezia studies with UCLA Institutional Review Boards approval].
in_text_mentions: Colonoscopic findings in patients with transient colitis and reversible colopathy are associated with mucosal or submucosal ischemic injury. These include segmental erythema and edematous mucosa, petechial hemorrhages, erosions, non-necrotic ulceration, and/or longitudinal ulcerations. In those with gangrenous colitis, colonoscopic findings include cyanotic mucosa and pseudopolyps [18]. Figure 1 shows colonoscopic findings of ischemic colitis, ranging from mild erythema to gangrenous mucosa.

copic severity into 3 stages [26]. Stage I includes patchy erythema, erosions, and small ulcerations with ischemia limited to the mucosa. Stage II includes larger and deeper non-necrotic ulcerations with ischemia limited to the submucosa. Stage III includes necrotic, gangrenous, and a possible perforated colon due to transmural injury [26]. The Favier classification is clinically useful in diagnosing and assessing the prognosis of IC and the need for surgery. Patients with stage III (IC in Figure 1) are associated with a high risk of requiring colon surgery and longer hospital stay [23,26–28].

panels.rationale: Single axial contrast-enhanced abdominal CT from a real patient with embolic inferior mesenteric artery occlusion in the acute phase of ischemic colitis. The image visibly shows left colonic wall thickening with a target/"little rose" mural attenuation pattern (straight white arrow) and adjacent pericolic fluid (curved white arrow), which are classic CT manifestations of acute ischemic colitis. The endoscopy and histology phrases in the caption describe companion findings not depicted in this CT panel, so only the CT-visible target sign is tagged; pericolic fluid and wall thickening are added as proposed findings. Prior caption triage confirms a real patient radiology image with no third-party restriction. [raw subtype: embolic]
panels.attribution_text: Iacobellis et al. CT findings in acute, subacute, and chronic ischemic colitis: suggestions for diagnosis.. BioMed research international 2014. doi:10.1155/2014/895248. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Patients with embolic IMA occlusion in acute phase: left colonic wall thickening (white arrow) with evidence of “little rose” sign or target aspect after i.v. contrast medium administration was detected; pericolic fluid was also present (curved arrow); the endoscopy showed edematous and thickened mucosa with diffuse petechial hemorrhage and hemorrhagic nodules; in some segments also hemorrhagic ulcerations were detected. These findings were histologically related to vascular congestion with intraparietal haemorrhage and increased cellularity with the presence of reactive inflammatory cells.
in_text_mentions: the disease, which, in the AP, was due to a colonic acute ischemic injury caused by IMA occlusion rapidly followed by reperfusion of the involved tract from Riolan's arcade's collateral vessels (Figure 2). The unenhanced phase may detect any hemorrhagic phenomenon of the bowel wall; in our patients, this finding was observed as bowel wall hyperdensity in 43.8% of patients in AP. Mucosal hyperdensity from hemorrhagic phenomena may determine a typical feature, the “little rose” sign [34] (Figure 3). In AP, pneumatosis was detected as late and severe sign of bowel infarction in only one patient.

panels.rationale: Single coronal contrast-enhanced CT panel of a real patient with acute occlusive ischemic colitis (explicit caption and article title). The arrow marks segmental descending (left) colonic wall thickening with disappearance of the lumen and mucosal hyperperfusion — a classic watershed-distribution CT presentation of IC; the layered mural attenuation supports the target sign, corroborated by the caption's histology description of mural edema and hemorrhage. The endoscopy and histology findings also described in the caption are not depicted in this image and are therefore not tagged. Dark bubbles adjacent to the affected segment are not definitively intramural pneumatosis from the image alone, so pneumatosis is not tagged. [raw subtype: occlusive]

panels.figure_caption: Contrast-enhanced CT in patients with acute occlusive IC: homogeneous left colonic involvement with disappearance of the lumen (arrow) and hyperperfusion of the mucosa in coronal plane. The endoscopy showed the presence of thickened mucosa with hemorrhagic phenomena. The histological findings were represented by increased thickness of the entire mucosal layer with intraparietal edema with hemorrhage and reactive inflammatory cells.

in_text_mentions: pic examination revealed various histopathological features in the colon. The pathological process affected both the mucosa and submucosa. Ulcerations were present in the mucosa, accompanied by architectural distortions, a reduction in the size and number of crypts, or their complete absence. Edema, foci of hemorrhage, and pink hyaline material were observed in the lamina propria. Vascular congestion, focal microthrombi, and chronic inflammation were noted in the mucosa, extending into the submucosa. In other sections, necrosis was observed extending into the submucosa (Figure 5 and Figure 6).

panels.rationale: Coronal CT angiogram of a real patient from a case report of ischemic colitis. The caption and in-text explicitly describe poor contrast filling of the distal branches of the left colic artery (blue arrow), poorly perfused vas recta, and overall poor bowel wall enhancement, and the accompanying text states these findings were possibly accompanied by ischemic colitis, later confirmed by colonoscopy and biopsy. The left colic artery territory corresponds to a watershed zone (Griffiths point/splenic flexure), and the poor bowel wall enhancement is a recognized CT manifestation of ischemic colitis. No third-party copyright, no other disease, no diagram or control content.

in_text_mentions: The histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of ischemic colitis describing colonic mucosa with surface epithelial degeneration, areas of mucosal necrosis and loss of superficial portions of glands (“withering crypts”). Lamina propria showed hyalinization, capillary congestion, focal hemorrhage, and reduced acute inflammation. The crypts were mucin depleted and the lining epithelium presented nuclear reactive changes consisting of nuclear hyperchromasia and enlargement, along with an increased number of mitotic figures (Figure 2A–C).

in_text_mentions: tions. She was afebrile and her vital signs were stable. Physical examination revealed a soft, flat abdomen with localized tenderness in the left flank, but no signs of peritoneal irritation. Laboratory tests showed a hemoglobin level of 13.4 g/dL, a WBC count of 9200/µL, and a CRP level of 0.09 mg/dL, indicating no anemia or inflammatory response. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated colonic wall thickening with increased pericolic fat density (dirty fat sign) around the splenic flexure, without evidence of mesenteric vessel occlusion (Fig. 1A). She was admitted with a diagnosis of IC.

Laboratory findings revealed a WBC count of 7200/µL and a CRP level of 5.65 mg/dL, indicating only a mild inflammatory response. On hospital day 4, her abdominal pain worsened, and signs of peritoneal irritation appeared. Blood tests revealed marked elevations of her WBC count (10400/µL) and CRP level (37.32 mg/dL). Repeat contrast-enhanced CT showed localized areas of poor enhancement in the colonic wall at the splenic flexure and descending colon, with no evidence of perforation (Fig. 1B). These findings raised concern for the progression to gangrenous IC, and emergency surgery was planned.

in_text_mentions: nterological evaluation and an urgent colonoscopy, which revealed severe inflammation with ulceration and friability in the distal transverse colon and splenic flexure. Passage of the scope beyond this region was not possible due to severe narrowing, colonic ulceration, and inflammation (Figure 2). The patient demonstrated only mild inflammation in the sigmoid colon and rectum. Colonic diverticulosis was observed in the descending colon, along with moderate external hemorrhoids. The caption and in-text explicitly attribute this to ischemic colitis, and the disease-focused article title ('Gangrenous ischemic colitis localized to the cecum') with the in-text diagnosis of hemorrhagic necrosis of the cecum directly supports the gangrenous subtype and cecum body site. Characteristic textbook presentation. [raw subtype: gangrenous] b: H&E histopathology of the same resected cecum specimen showing inflammatory cell infiltration with neutrophils in the inflamed areas, supporting acute inflammation in ischemic colitis per the caption and in-text ('Full-thickness inflammatory cell infiltration consisting predominantly of neutrophils... indicating acute inflammation'). The neutrophilic infiltrate is not in the allowed...

panels.rationale: Single axial contrast CT of the abdomen/pelvis from a case report titled 'Stercoral colitis complicated with ischemic colitis.' The image shows a large retained-stool burden in the colon with bowel wall thickening (arrow) and pericolonic fat stranding. The bowel wall thickening on contrast CT is interpreted as mural edema (target sign) attributable to the ischemic colitis complicating the stercoral disease, supported by the disease-focused article title and the prior caption triage (route: keep). Confidence is moderate because the CT findings are nonspecific and overlap with stercoral colitis itself; no watershed distribution, explicit target/halo attenuation, pneumatosis, or perforation is described (in-text is negative for intramural air/abscess).

Additionally, the surrounding fat gaps exhibited vague oozing.

panels.rationale: Single H&E histology image (100x) of a transverse colon biopsy from a patient with amoxicillin-clavulanate-induced ischemic colitis. The left portion of the field shows crypts with decreased mucin vacuoles (attenuated/withered crypts) and a hemorrhagic, fibrotic lamina propria, while the right portion shows normal mucosa as an internal contrast within the same biopsy field. Caption and in-text explicitly attribute these histologic changes to ischemic colitis. The normal mucosa is an in-image contrast, not a separate control panel, so the image qualifies as a real patient image showing specific ischemic colitis manifestations.

in_text_mentions: Given his clinical presentation and concern for active lower gastrointestinal bleeding, he was admitted for endoscopic evaluation. A colonoscopy showed erythema in the sigmoid colon and approximately 30 cm of circumferential edema and erythema without ulceration in the transverse and descending colon (Figure 2), with clearly demarcated edges straddled by normal mucosa (Figure 3). Colonic biopsies (Figure 4) showed decreased mucin vacuoles, attenuated crypts, and a hemorrhagic and fibrotic lamina propria, consistent with ischemic colitis.

Appendicitis was suspected and the patient was referred to an abdominal ultrasound, which revealed a typical case of isolated right sided ischemic colitis (Figure 1(a)). Due to the young age of the patient he was questioned about ongoing drug abuse linking cocaine abuse to ischemic colitis. Detailed history revealed a drug abuse including the use of intravenous cocaine several times weekly during the last three months. The patient described intermittent and self-limiting abdominal pain and vomiting during the same period. The most recent cocaine admi

Based on the clinical assessment and diagnostic imaging appendicitis could be ruled out. A subsequent contrast enhanced abdominal computed tomography showed an inflamed ascending colon and cecum possibly extending into the terminal ileum (Figure 1(b)).

To confirm the diagnosis and to rule out Crohn's disease the patient underwent a colonoscopy. The ascending colon (Figure 1(c)) and cecum (Figure 1(d)) showed ulcerations whereas the remaining colon appeared normal. Histology on the biopsies revealed changes consistent with ischemic colitis without signs of inflammatory bowel disease or malignancy.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Coronal oblique CT reconstruction clearly shows segmental wall thickening of the left colon (descending/sigmoid) with a sharp transition to normal transverse colon wall, consistent with watershed-zone ischemic colitis. Real human patient imaging with high diagnostic quality. B: Axial venous-phase CT demonstrates stratified (target/halo) wall thickening of the proximal sigmoid, a classic CT finding of ischemic colitis reflecting mural edema and submucosal hemorrhage. Real human patient imaging. C: Sagittal CT reconstruction confirms symmetrical wall thickening localized to the left colon (descending/sigmoid), consistent with watershed-zone ischemic colitis. Real human patient imaging with clear anatomical detail.

in_text_mentions: Consequently, we continued to investigate the patient with a computed tomography (CT) which showed a symmetrically thickened colonic wall corresponding to the descending and sigmoid segments, without obvious stenosis and without dilation of the proximal segments. The colonic vascularization on CT scan was negative for arterial or venous thromboses and the presence of the Comb sign was supportive of a local inflammatory process (Figure 3A–C).

panels.rationale: Single axial contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis from a case report titled 'Gut Trouble: A Rare Case of Amoxicillin-Clavulanate-Induced Ischemic Colitis in a Young Adult.' Arrows indicate bowel thickening and mucosal hyperemia involving the transverse and descending colon and splenic flexure — a watershed distribution characteristic of ischemic colitis. Real patient image, no third-party copyright, prior triage kept it; disease attribution supported by the disease-focused article title plus the specific captioned CT manifestation.

Contrast-enhanced CT imaging demonstrated bowel thickening and mucosal hyperemia of the splenic flexure (Figure 1).

plate_findings.evidence: in-text states contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed thickening and hypoenhancement of the descending and sigmoid colon

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Coronal contrast-enhanced abdominal CT from the disease-focused ischemic colitis article; the in-text specifically describes thickening and hypoenhancement of the descending and sigmoid colon in this patient. B: Axial CT/CTA in the same ischemic colitis case; the arrow/asterisk mark the mesenteric AVM nidus, and the in-text links that AVM to the ischemic colitis diagnosis while also describing colonic hypoenhancement. C: Coronal CT/CTA from the ischemic colitis case shows the described descending/sigmoid bowel hypoenhancement and the mesenteric AVM vasculature tied to the diagnosis in the disease-focused title and in-text. D: Volume-rendered CT angiogram is real patient imaging, not a schematic; it shows the inferior mesenteric artery-to-vein AVM that the disease-focused title and in-text name as the rare cause of this patient's ischemic colitis. AVM findings are not in the provided vocabulary, so they are proposed.
panels.attribution_text: Kanacharoen et al. Ischemic Colitis Secondary to Mesenteric Arteriovenous Malformation: A Rare Cause of Bowel Ischemia-Case Report and Literature Review.. DEN open 2026. doi:10.1002/deo2.70289. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Findings of arteriovenous malformation from the computerized tomography of the abdomen and the computerized tomography angiogram in this case.
in_text_mentions: e colitis extended beyond the classical watershed regions. Biopsies during colonoscopy revealed epithelial erosion and chronic active inflammation with reactive atypia. A contrast‐enhanced abdominal CT (Figures 2 and 3) done three days post‐admission revealed thickening and hypoenhancement of the descending and sigmoid colon. CT angiography identified an AVM originating from the IMA and draining into the IMV via a dilated outflow vein with a prominent vascular nidus, which was consistent with mesenteric steal physiology. This led to the diagnosis of ischemic colitis caused by a mesenteric AVM.
